The refractory period is set by Na+ channel inactivation and is not a target of presynaptic modulation.

cards.q: What is the main advantage of presynaptic control over postsynaptic control?
cards.a: Selectivity, because only one input to the target cell is changed.
options: Speed, because it acts before the action potential arrives
Selectivity, because only one input to the target cell is changed
Strength, because it always abolishes the response completely
Permanence, because its effect cannot be reversed
cards.explanation: Acting on a single terminal turns one input up or down while every other input to the same neuron continues unchanged, which is the point of the arrangement. It is not faster, since it still requires transmitter release and second messenger action at the terminal. It is graded rather than all or nothing. Its effect is reversible and lasts only as long as the modulating input is active.

cards.q: How does postsynaptic inhibition act on the target neuron?
cards.a: It produces an IPSP that reduces the effect of every excitatory input to that cell.
options: It produces an IPSP that reduces the effect of every excitatory input to that cell
It reduces transmitter release from one selected presynaptic terminal and leaves the others alone
It removes receptors from a single dendritic spine
It blocks conduction along the presynaptic axon before the signal can arrive
cards.explanation: An inhibitory synapse on the soma or dendrite changes the membrane potential and conductance of the target cell, so all excitatory currents converging on that cell are opposed. Reducing release from one terminal is presynaptic inhibition. Removing receptors from a single spine is a plasticity mechanism, not classic postsynaptic inhibition. Blocking axonal conduction is not how synaptic inhibition works.

cards.q: Which receptor on a presynaptic terminal is commonly responsible for presynaptic inhibition in the central nervous system?
cards.a: The GABA-B receptor.
options: The nicotinic receptor
The AMPA receptor
The NMDA receptor
The GABA-B receptor
cards.explanation: GABA-B receptors on terminals act through G proteins to reduce Ca2+ channel opening and increase K+ conductance, cutting release from that terminal. Nicotinic receptors are excitatory cation channels. AMPA and NMDA receptors are the excitatory glutamate receptors of the postsynaptic membrane and do not mediate this inhibition.

cards.q: A modulating neuron activates GABA-B receptors on an excitatory terminal, reducing Ca2+ channel opening there. What does the postsynaptic cell record?
cards.a: A smaller EPSP from that input, with no change in resting potential.
options: A larger EPSP from that input, with no change in resting potential
A smaller EPSP from that input, with no change in resting potential
A hyperpolarization of the resting potential with normal EPSPs
A complete loss of all synaptic input to the cell
cards.explanation: Less Ca2+ entry means less transmitter from that terminal, so that one EPSP shrinks while the postsynaptic membrane itself is untouched and rests where it always did. A larger EPSP would follow from facilitation. A shift in resting potential is the fingerprint of postsynaptic inhibition. Other inputs to the cell are unaffected, which is the whole advantage of the presynaptic route.

cards.q: A neuron receives five excitatory inputs, and a circuit needs to suppress only the third one while leaving the other four intact. Which arrangement accomplishes this?
cards.a: Presynaptic inhibition at the terminal of input three.
options: Presynaptic inhibition at the terminal of input three
Postsynaptic inhibition at the soma
An IPSP at the axon hillock
Blocking the postsynaptic receptor shared by all five inputs
cards.explanation: Only an axoaxonic contact on that one terminal changes that one input, which is what selectivity means. Postsynaptic inhibition at the soma damps every input at once. An IPSP at the hillock is even less selective, since it sits where all currents converge. Blocking a shared receptor would weaken all five inputs together.

cards.q: During presynaptic inhibition of one input, what happens to the resting membrane potential and input resistance of the postsynaptic neuron?
cards.a: Both are unchanged, because nothing opens on the postsynaptic membrane.
options: The resting potential falls and the input resistance falls
The resting potential rises and the input resistance rises
Both are unchanged, because nothing opens on the postsynaptic membrane
The resting potential is unchanged but the input resistance falls sharply
cards.explanation: Presynaptic inhibition acts entirely on the terminal, so the postsynaptic membrane opens no new channels and both its resting potential and its resistance stay put. A drop in both is what postsynaptic inhibition produces when Cl- or K+ channels open. A rise in resting potential and resistance does not follow from either mechanism. A resistance drop alone is the signature of shunting inhibition on the postsynaptic membrane.

cards.q: A facilitating neuron blocks K+ channels in an axon terminal, so the terminal action potential lasts longer. Predict the effect on transmitter release from that terminal.
cards.a: Release increases, because Ca2+ channels stay open longer.
options: Release decreases, because the terminal cannot repolarize
Release stops, because the terminal becomes refractory
Release is unchanged, because K+ does not affect vesicles
Release increases, because Ca2+ channels stay open longer
cards.explanation: Prolonging the depolarization keeps voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open longer, terminal Ca2+ rises higher, and more vesicles fuse. Slower repolarization increases rather than decreases release. K+ channels do not touch vesicles directly, but they set how long the terminal stays depolarized, which is what matters. Terminals do not enter a refractory block from a single lengthened spike.

cards.q: An opioid peptide reduces pain signaling by acting on receptors located on the terminals of pain afferents. How should this modulation be classified?
cards.a: Presynaptic inhibition, because it reduces release from a selected terminal.
options: Postsynaptic inhibition, because the second order neuron hyperpolarizes
Presynaptic inhibition, because it reduces release from a selected terminal
Presynaptic facilitation, because it changes release from a terminal
Spatial summation, because several inputs are combined
cards.explanation: The receptor sits on the terminal and the effect is less transmitter released, which is presynaptic inhibition acting on one specific input. Postsynaptic inhibition would require the modulation to change the membrane potential of the second order neuron itself. Facilitation would increase release rather than reduce it. Summation describes adding postsynaptic potentials, not modulating release.

cards.q: A recording from a postsynaptic neuron shows a smaller EPSP from input A, while its resting potential, its input resistance, and its response to directly applied transmitter are all normal. EPSPs from inputs B and C are also normal. Where is the modulation acting?
cards.a: Presynaptically, on the terminal of input A.
options: Postsynaptically, on the receptors shared by all inputs
On the axon of the postsynaptic neuron
Postsynaptically, at the axon hillock
Presynaptically, on the terminal of input A
cards.explanation: An unchanged postsynaptic membrane and an unchanged response to applied transmitter rule out the postsynaptic side, and the fact that only input A is weakened points to its terminal specifically. A change in shared receptors would weaken B and C too. A hillock effect would change the whole cell's excitability rather than one EPSP. The postsynaptic axon carries output and does not shape the size of an incoming EPSP.

cards.q: In a second experiment on the same kind of neuron, the resting potential shifts from -70 mV to -76 mV, the input resistance falls, and EPSPs from all three inputs shrink by the same proportion. What is happening?
cards.a: Postsynaptic inhibition, opening channels on the target cell membrane.
options: Postsynaptic inhibition, opening channels on the target cell membrane
Presynaptic inhibition at all three terminals at once
Presynaptic facilitation at one terminal
Loss of the presynaptic action potential in all three of the axons
cards.explanation: A hyperpolarized resting potential together with lower input resistance means new channels opened on the postsynaptic membrane, and their shunting effect scales down every input equally. Presynaptic inhibition at all three terminals would shrink the EPSPs but leave the resting potential and resistance untouched. Facilitation would enlarge an EPSP. Loss of the presynaptic spikes would abolish the EPSPs rather than shrink them proportionally.

cards.q: A drug destroys the axoaxonic synapse that had been inhibiting one of four excitatory inputs to a neuron. Predict what happens to the four inputs and to the firing of the cell.
cards.a: That one input grows stronger, the other three are unchanged, and the cell is more likely to fire.
options: All four of the excitatory inputs grow stronger together, and the cell fires far more often than it did before
That one input weakens further and the cell fires less often
That one input grows stronger, the other three are unchanged, and the cell is more likely to fire
The resting potential depolarizes by several millivolts and all four of the inputs shrink
cards.explanation: Removing a selective brake restores full release at that single terminal, which is exactly the selectivity that presynaptic control provides, and the extra excitatory current makes threshold easier to reach. All four strengthening would require the lost inhibition to have been postsynaptic. Losing an inhibitor cannot weaken the input it was suppressing. The postsynaptic resting potential was never changed by presynaptic inhibition, so it does not shift when that inhibition is removed.

cards.q: What is long term potentiation?
cards.a: A lasting increase in synaptic strength that follows brief high frequency stimulation.
options: A lasting decrease in synaptic strength that follows a prolonged period of synaptic inactivity
A brief increase in transmitter release that lasts only a few milliseconds
A lasting increase in synaptic strength that follows brief high frequency stimulation
A permanent change in the resting potential of a neuron
cards.explanation: After a short burst of high frequency stimulation, the same test stimulus produces a larger response for hours or longer, which is why LTP is treated as a cellular model of learning. A change lasting milliseconds is short term facilitation, not potentiation. A lasting decrease is long term depression, the mirror process. LTP changes the strength of specific synapses rather than the cell's resting potential.

cards.q: In which brain region has long term potentiation been studied most thoroughly?
cards.a: The hippocampus.
options: The cerebellum
The hypothalamus
The medulla oblongata
The hippocampus
cards.explanation: Hippocampal circuits are laid out in orderly layers and are central to forming new memories, which made them the standard preparation for studying LTP. The cerebellum shows its own plasticity, better known for long term depression. The medulla handles autonomic reflexes such as breathing and blood pressure. The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis and endocrine output.

cards.q: Which receptor acts as the coincidence detector in long term potentiation?
cards.a: The NMDA receptor.
options: The NMDA receptor
The GABA-A receptor
The AMPA receptor
The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
cards.explanation: The NMDA receptor opens only when glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic membrane is already depolarized, so it reports that presynaptic and postsynaptic activity happened together. AMPA receptors open on glutamate binding alone and carry the ordinary fast EPSP. GABA-A receptors are inhibitory Cl- channels. Nicotinic receptors respond to acetylcholine and are not part of this pathway.

cards.q: Which ion blocks the NMDA receptor channel while the postsynaptic membrane is at its resting potential?
cards.a: Mg2+.
options: K+
Mg2+
Cl-
HCO3-
cards.explanation: Mg2+ sits in the pore at negative membrane potentials and is expelled when the membrane depolarizes, which is the voltage dependence that makes the receptor a coincidence detector. K+ moves through many channels but does not plug the NMDA pore. Cl- passes through inhibitory receptor channels. HCO3- matters in acid base handling and has no role here.

cards.q: Which ion enters through the open NMDA receptor and triggers the changes that produce long term potentiation?
cards.a: Ca2+.
options: Cl-
Mg2+
Ca2+
H+
cards.explanation: NMDA receptor channels are unusual among glutamate receptors in passing Ca2+, and the rise in postsynaptic Ca2+ activates the kinases that strengthen the synapse. Cl- entry is inhibitory and does not pass this channel. Mg2+ blocks the channel rather than acting as the signal. H+ movement is not the trigger for plasticity.

cards.q: Which receptor is inserted into the postsynaptic membrane during the expression of long term potentiation?
cards.a: The AMPA receptor.
options: The AMPA receptor
The muscarinic receptor
The GABA-B receptor
The glycine receptor
cards.explanation: More AMPA receptors in the membrane means the same amount of released glutamate opens more channels and the EPSP is larger, which is how the strengthening is expressed. GABA-B receptors mediate slow inhibition and presynaptic damping. Muscarinic receptors respond to acetylcholine. Glycine receptors are inhibitory Cl- channels of the cord and brainstem.

cards.q: Which neurotransmitter is released at the synapses where long term potentiation is classically studied?
cards.a: Glutamate.
options: GABA
Glutamate
Acetylcholine
Norepinephrine
cards.explanation: These are excitatory glutamate synapses, and glutamate acting at both AMPA and NMDA receptors is what makes the coincidence detection possible. GABA is inhibitory and is not the transmitter at these synapses. Acetylcholine and norepinephrine modulate hippocampal circuits but are not the transmitter carrying the potentiated signal.

cards.q: What is long term depression?
cards.a: A lasting decrease in synaptic strength, typically after prolonged low frequency stimulation.
options: A failure of transmitter release caused by depletion of the vesicle pool during a long period of heavy activity
A brief hyperpolarization following an action potential
A lasting decrease in the resting membrane potential of the presynaptic neuron
A lasting decrease in synaptic strength, typically after prolonged low frequency stimulation
cards.explanation: Low frequency stimulation, often around 1 Hz for several minutes, weakens the synapse durably, largely by removing AMPA receptors from the postsynaptic membrane. A brief hyperpolarization after a spike is the afterhyperpolarization, a K+ current effect. Long term depression is about synaptic strength, not about a shifted resting potential. Vesicle depletion is a short term effect that recovers within seconds.

cards.q: What two conditions must be met at the same time for the NMDA receptor channel to open and pass current?
cards.a: Glutamate must be bound and the postsynaptic membrane must be depolarized.
options: GABA must be bound and the presynaptic terminal must be depolarized
Glutamate must be bound and the postsynaptic membrane must be hyperpolarized
Glutamate must be bound and the postsynaptic membrane must be depolarized
Glycine must be bound and extracellular Ca2+ must be low
cards.explanation: Binding alone leaves the pore plugged by Mg2+, and depolarization alone gives nothing to open the gate, so both must occur together, which is what makes the receptor a detector of coincident activity. Hyperpolarization drives Mg2+ further into the pore and closes it more firmly. GABA does not act at this receptor. Glycine does serve as a co agonist, but the requirement being tested here is glutamate plus depolarization.

cards.q: A postsynaptic membrane depolarizes strongly during a burst of stimulation. What does this do at NMDA receptors that have glutamate bound?
cards.a: Mg2+ leaves the pore and Ca2+ flows into the cell.
options: Mg2+ leaves the pore and Ca2+ flows into the cell
Mg2+ enters the pore and current stops
Cl- flows into the cell and the synapse weakens
The receptor is removed from the membrane
cards.explanation: Depolarization pushes the positively charged Mg2+ out of the pore, unblocking the channel so that Na+ and Ca2+ can enter, and the Ca2+ signal starts the potentiating cascade. Mg2+ block deepens with hyperpolarization, not depolarization. NMDA receptor channels are cation channels and do not pass Cl-. Receptor removal from the membrane is a feature of long term depression rather than of unblocking.

cards.q: A drug prevents new AMPA receptors from being inserted into the postsynaptic membrane. High frequency stimulation is then delivered. What is the predicted result?
cards.a: Ca2+ still enters through NMDA receptors, but the EPSP does not grow.
options: The synapse is silenced completely
No Ca2+ enters and the EPSP does not grow
The EPSP grows normally, since receptor insertion is not required for this
Ca2+ still enters through NMDA receptors, but the EPSP does not grow
cards.explanation: Blocking insertion leaves the trigger intact, so the Ca2+ signal still occurs, but the expression step that would enlarge the response is missing. Ca2+ entry is an NMDA receptor event and is not prevented by an insertion blocker. Insertion of AMPA receptors is a main route by which the strengthening is expressed, so its loss matters. Existing AMPA receptors still work, so baseline transmission continues.

cards.q: After potentiation, the same amount of glutamate produces a larger EPSP at a synapse. What postsynaptic change best explains this?
cards.a: More AMPA receptors are present in the postsynaptic membrane.
options: Fewer AMPA receptors are present in the postsynaptic membrane
More AMPA receptors are present in the postsynaptic membrane
The Mg2+ block of the NMDA receptor has become permanent
The postsynaptic cell has hyperpolarized
cards.explanation: If the transmitter amount is fixed and the response is bigger, the postsynaptic side must be more responsive, and inserting AMPA receptors is the classic way that happens. Fewer receptors would shrink the response. A permanent Mg2+ block would abolish NMDA current and prevent future plasticity rather than enlarge the ordinary EPSP. Hyperpolarization would increase driving force somewhat but does not account for a lasting change of this kind.

cards.q: A synapse is stimulated at 1 Hz for fifteen minutes. What is the expected outcome?
cards.a: Long term depression, with AMPA receptors removed from the membrane.
options: Long term depression, with AMPA receptors removed from the membrane
Long term potentiation, with AMPA receptors added to the membrane
No change at all, because the stimulation is too weak to matter
Presynaptic facilitation lasting several minutes
cards.explanation: Prolonged low frequency stimulation produces a small sustained rise in postsynaptic Ca2+ that favors phosphatases over kinases and drives receptor removal, weakening the synapse. Potentiation requires the brief, intense Ca2+ rise that only high frequency stimulation delivers. This protocol changes the synapse durably rather than leaving it untouched. Presynaptic facilitation requires a modulating input at the terminal, which is not part of this protocol.

cards.q: Why does a single presynaptic action potential fail to induce long term potentiation, while a rapid train succeeds?
cards.a: Only the train depolarizes the postsynaptic cell enough to relieve the Mg2+ block.
options: Only the train releases enough glutamate to occupy the AMPA receptors at the synapse
Only the train reaches the presynaptic terminal
Only the train depolarizes the postsynaptic cell enough to relieve the Mg2+ block
Only the train causes transmitter to diffuse all the way across the synaptic cleft
cards.explanation: A single EPSP is too small to move the membrane far from rest, so Mg2+ stays in the NMDA pore, while a train summates to a large depolarization that unblocks the channel and lets Ca2+ in. A single spike releases plenty of glutamate to bind AMPA receptors, which is why a normal EPSP appears. Single action potentials do reach the terminal. Diffusion across the cleft happens with every release event.

cards.q: High frequency stimulation is delivered while an NMDA receptor blocker is present. No potentiation develops. After the blocker is washed out, the baseline EPSP is normal. What does this experiment show?
cards.a: NMDA receptor activation is required to induce potentiation but not to carry ordinary transmission.
options: AMPA receptors are the receptors required to induce potentiation
Potentiation depends on the amount of transmitter released rather than on the postsynaptic receptors at all
The presynaptic terminal was damaged by the stimulation
NMDA receptor activation is required to induce potentiation but not to carry ordinary transmission
cards.explanation: A normal baseline EPSP with the blocker removed proves the synapse works through AMPA receptors, and the failure to potentiate while NMDA receptors were blocked places the induction requirement squarely on them. AMPA receptors carry the baseline response and express the strengthening, but they are not the induction trigger. A damaged terminal would leave the baseline EPSP small. The experiment specifically implicates a postsynaptic receptor.

cards.q: The postsynaptic cell is voltage clamped at -70 mV during a high frequency train, so it cannot depolarize. Glutamate release is normal. Predict whether potentiation develops and explain the result.
cards.a: No potentiation, because Mg2+ remains in the NMDA pore and Ca2+ cannot enter.
options: Potentiation develops normally, because glutamate release is what matters
No potentiation, because Mg2+ remains in the NMDA pore and Ca2+ cannot enter
No potentiation, because glutamate cannot be released at -70 mV
Potentiation develops but is expressed presynaptically instead
cards.explanation: Holding the membrane at rest keeps the voltage dependent Mg2+ block in place, so even with glutamate bound the NMDA channel stays shut and the Ca2+ trigger never arrives. Release alone is not enough, which is exactly why the receptor is called a coincidence detector. Presynaptic release is unaffected by clamping the postsynaptic cell. Nothing about the clamp redirects expression to the terminal, since induction itself failed.

cards.q: A chemical that binds calcium tightly is injected into the postsynaptic neuron before a high frequency train. Transmitter release and NMDA channel opening are both normal, but no potentiation develops. What does this identify?
cards.a: A rise in postsynaptic Ca2+ is the trigger for potentiation.
options: Presynaptic Ca2+ entry is the trigger for potentiation
Glutamate binding alone is sufficient to trigger potentiation
A rise in postsynaptic Ca2+ is the trigger for potentiation
Mg2+ entry into the postsynaptic cell is the trigger for potentiation
cards.explanation: Everything upstream worked and only the postsynaptic Ca2+ signal was removed, so that signal is the necessary trigger for the cascade that strengthens the synapse. Presynaptic Ca2+ entry was normal, since release was normal, and the injected buffer stayed in the postsynaptic cell. Glutamate binding was also normal and clearly was not sufficient. Mg2+ leaves the pore during depolarization rather than serving as the signal.

cards.q: Two pathways converge on one hippocampal neuron. A weak pathway is stimulated alone and produces no lasting change. When the same weak stimulation is paired with strong stimulation of the other pathway, the weak pathway is potentiated. What accounts for this?
cards.a: The strong pathway depolarized the cell, unblocking NMDA receptors at the weak pathway's active synapses.
options: The strong pathway increased transmitter release at the terminals belonging to the weak pathway during the pairing
The strong pathway depolarized the cell, unblocking NMDA receptors at the weak pathway's active synapses
The weak pathway switched its transmitter to glutamate during pairing
The strong pathway removed AMPA receptors from the synapses made by the weak pathway
cards.explanation: Depolarization is a property of the whole postsynaptic cell, so the strong input supplies the voltage while the weak input supplies the glutamate, and only synapses receiving both meet the coincidence requirement. There is no axoaxonic contact described that would raise release at the weak terminals. Neurons do not swap transmitters over the course of an experiment. Removing AMPA receptors would weaken the synapse, the opposite of the result observed.

cards.q: What structure joins the two cells at an electrical synapse?
cards.a: A gap junction.
options: A synaptic cleft of 20 to 40 nm
A tight junction
A desmosome
A gap junction
cards.explanation: A gap junction is a set of paired channels that lines up across a 2 to 4 nm gap and creates a continuous pore between the cytoplasm of the two cells. A tight junction seals the space between cells and blocks leakage rather than conducting current. A desmosome is a mechanical anchor. A wide cleft of 20 to 40 nm is the arrangement at a chemical synapse.

cards.q: Which protein forms the channels of a gap junction?
cards.a: Connexin.
options: Connexin
Actin
Synaptotagmin
Dystrophin
cards.explanation: Six connexin subunits form a connexon in each membrane, and two connexons align to make one continuous pore. Actin is a cytoskeletal filament. Synaptotagmin is the vesicle calcium sensor at chemical synapses. Dystrophin links the muscle cytoskeleton to the membrane and is unrelated to junctional channels.

cards.q: In which direction does current usually flow at an electrical synapse?
cards.a: In either direction, since the junction is usually bidirectional.
options: Only in one direction, from the presynaptic to the postsynaptic cell
Only in one direction, from the postsynaptic back to the presynaptic cell
In either direction, since the junction is usually bidirectional
Only when both of the coupled cells are hyperpolarized
cards.explanation: The pore is an open channel between two cytoplasms, so current flows whichever way the voltage difference drives it, and either cell can influence the other. One way transmission is the rule at chemical synapses, where transmitter is released from only one side. Restricting flow to a single direction in either sense misses the symmetry of the junction. Current flows whenever a voltage difference exists, not only during hyperpolarization.

cards.q: About how long is the synaptic delay at an electrical synapse?
cards.a: Essentially zero.
options: About 0.5 ms
About 2 ms
About 10 ms
Essentially zero
cards.explanation: Current passes directly through the open junction, so there is no release step and no measurable delay. A delay near 0.5 ms is the value at a fast chemical synapse, where Ca2+ entry and vesicle fusion take time. Two milliseconds and ten milliseconds are longer than even most chemical synapses require.

cards.q: What passes from one cell to the other through a gap junction channel?
cards.a: Ions and small molecules, carrying current directly.
options: Ions and small molecules, carrying current directly
Neurotransmitter that is still packaged inside its vesicles
Whole proteins and small organelles
Only water molecules and nothing else
cards.explanation: The pore is wide enough for ions and small molecules up to about 1000 daltons, so charge moves directly and the two cells share second messengers as well. Vesicles are not transferred at any synapse. The pore is far too narrow for proteins or organelles. Water can cross, but restricting the list to water would leave out the ion flow that makes the junction electrically useful.

cards.q: In which tissue are electrical synapses at gap junctions essential for normal function?
cards.a: Cardiac muscle.
options: Skeletal muscle fibers
Cardiac muscle
The neuromuscular junction
Myelinated peripheral axons
cards.explanation: Gap junctions in the intercalated discs let cardiac muscle cells depolarize as one unit, which is what allows the coordinated contraction of a chamber. Skeletal muscle fibers are electrically separate and each is driven by its own motor neuron. The neuromuscular junction is a chemical synapse using acetylcholine. Myelinated axons conduct along their own membrane and do not need gap junctions.

cards.q: Which type of synapse transmits faster, and what makes the difference?
cards.a: The electrical synapse, because current passes directly with no release step.
options: The chemical synapse, because transmitter diffuses faster than current flows
The chemical synapse, because it amplifies the signal
They are equally fast, since both depend on ion movement
The electrical synapse, because current passes directly with no release step
cards.explanation: Skipping Ca2+ entry, vesicle fusion, diffusion, and receptor binding removes essentially all of the delay, so an electrical synapse transmits almost instantly. Diffusion of a transmitter across a cleft is slower than direct current flow through an open pore. The two are not equally fast, since the chemical synapse adds the release steps. Amplification is a real advantage of chemical synapses, but it costs time rather than saving it.

cards.q: Which type of synapse allows more modulation of the signal, and why?
cards.a: The chemical synapse, because release, receptors, and clearance can each be adjusted.
options: The electrical synapse, because its gap junction channels are always open and freely conducting
Both equally, since both use voltage-gated channels
The chemical synapse, because release, receptors, and clearance can each be adjusted
The electrical synapse, because it can invert the sign of the signal it passes
cards.explanation: Every step of chemical transmission is a control point, so drugs, modulating neurons, and plasticity can turn the signal up, down, or off. Gap junction conductance can be adjusted somewhat by pH and Ca2+, but the range is narrow compared with a chemical synapse. Only the chemical synapse relies on the transmitter and receptor machinery that gives fine control. Inverting a signal, turning excitation into inhibition, is something only a chemical synapse does.

cards.q: A group of neurons must fire together in near perfect synchrony. Which arrangement best achieves this?
cards.a: Electrical synapses linking them through gap junctions.
options: Electrical synapses linking them through gap junctions
Chemical synapses that use glutamate as their transmitter at each contact
Chemical synapses that use GABA as their transmitter
Presynaptic inhibition acting among the members of the group
cards.explanation: Direct electrical coupling shares current instantly across the group, so the cells depolarize together and fire as a unit. Glutamate synapses would excite the group but each with its own synaptic delay, blurring the timing. GABA synapses would inhibit rather than synchronize firing. Presynaptic inhibition damps selected inputs and does nothing to synchronize.

cards.q: Extracellular Ca2+ is removed from a preparation containing both an electrical and a chemical synapse. What happens at each?
cards.a: The chemical synapse fails while the electrical synapse continues to transmit.
options: Both fail, since both depend on Ca2+ entry
The chemical synapse fails while the electrical synapse continues to transmit
The electrical synapse fails while the chemical synapse continues to transmit
Both continue, since neither depends on extracellular Ca2+
cards.explanation: Vesicle fusion requires Ca2+ entry, so removing external Ca2+ silences the chemical synapse, while the gap junction simply passes current and needs no Ca2+ trigger. The electrical synapse is the one that survives, not the one that fails. Chemical transmission is strictly Ca2+ dependent, so saying both continue is wrong.

cards.q: A signal passes through a chain of three electrically coupled cells and gets slightly smaller at each step, while a chemical synapse can produce a postsynaptic response larger than the presynaptic current. What does this comparison illustrate?
cards.a: Chemical synapses can amplify a signal, while electrical synapses cannot.
options: Electrical synapses can amplify a signal, while chemical synapses cannot
Neither type of synapse can change the size of a signal
Chemical synapses can amplify a signal, while electrical synapses cannot
Both types amplify equally, but at different speeds
cards.explanation: A chemical synapse spends energy to release many transmitter molecules that open many channels, so a small presynaptic signal can open a large postsynaptic current. An electrical synapse only divides existing current between the two cells, so the signal shrinks rather than grows. The chemical synapse clearly does change signal size. Equal amplification would erase the main functional difference between the two.

cards.q: Current injected into cell A produces an immediate small depolarization in cell B with no measurable delay. The response persists when extracellular Ca2+ is removed and when transmitter receptors are blocked. What kind of synapse joins these cells?
cards.a: An electrical synapse at a gap junction.
options: An electrical synapse at a gap junction
A chemical synapse using acetylcholine
A chemical synapse using glutamate
An axoaxonic synapse producing presynaptic inhibition
cards.explanation: No delay, survival without extracellular Ca2+, and indifference to receptor blockade all point to direct current flow through gap junction channels. A glutamate synapse would be abolished by receptor blockade. An acetylcholine synapse would be abolished by removing Ca2+, which stops release. Presynaptic inhibition modulates release at a chemical terminal and cannot explain a direct, immediate coupling.

cards.q: Two synapses are compared. Synapse X has a delay of about 1.5 ms and its response grows when an enzyme inhibitor is added to the cleft. Synapse Y has a delay too short to measure and is unaffected by the inhibitor. Identify each.
cards.a: X is chemical and Y is electrical.
options: Both are electrical, but X has fewer gap junctions
X is electrical and Y is chemical
Both are chemical, but Y uses a faster transmitter
X is chemical and Y is electrical
cards.explanation: A measurable delay plus sensitivity to an enzyme that clears transmitter identifies the chemical synapse, since only there does an enzyme shape the response. The absence of both features marks the electrical synapse. Calling X electrical reverses the two clearest pieces of evidence. No transmitter is fast enough to erase the delay, and no gap junction is affected by a cleft enzyme.

cards.q: Gap junctions between cardiac muscle cells are partially uncoupled by a change in intracellular pH. Predict the consequences for conduction through the ventricle.
cards.a: Current spreads less easily from cell to cell, so conduction slows and the contraction becomes less coordinated.
options: Conduction speeds up, because each cell now fires independently
Current spreads less easily from cell to cell, so conduction slows and the contraction becomes less coordinated
Conduction is unaffected, because cardiac muscle cells signal to one another through chemical synapses instead
Conduction stops immediately, because the gap junctions themselves carry the action potential from one cardiac cell to the next
cards.explanation: Cardiac cells depend on gap junctions to pass depolarizing current to their neighbors, so raising junctional resistance slows the spread and breaks up the coordinated wave of contraction. Independent firing would make conduction worse, not faster. Cardiac muscle cells are joined electrically rather than by chemical synapses. Partial uncoupling slows conduction rather than abolishing it, since each cell still regenerates its own action potential.

cards.q: In a synapse simulation, what does the vertical axis of the postsynaptic recording show?
cards.a: Membrane potential in mV.
options: Transmitter concentration in mmol/L
Current in nanoamperes through the stimulating electrode
Membrane potential in mV
Time in ms
cards.explanation: The postsynaptic trace plots the recorded membrane potential, which is why the baseline sits near -70 mV and events are read in millivolts. Transmitter concentration is a variable you set, not what the electrode reports. Stimulating current is an input to the presynaptic side. Time is plotted on the horizontal axis.

cards.q: Before any stimulus is delivered in the simulation, what value should the postsynaptic trace sit at?
cards.a: About -70 mV.
options: About -70 mV
About 0 mV
About +30 mV
About -90 mV
cards.explanation: The flat baseline before stimulation is the resting membrane potential, near -70 mV in a typical neuron. Zero millivolts would mean no charge separation across the membrane. A value near +30 mV is the peak of an action potential. A value near -90 mV is the K+ equilibrium potential, reached only during strong hyperpolarization.

cards.q: What does the stimulus frequency control in the simulation change?
cards.a: How many presynaptic action potentials are delivered per second.
options: The number of receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
How many presynaptic action potentials are delivered per second
The resting membrane potential of the postsynaptic neuron itself
The width of the synaptic cleft
cards.explanation: Frequency sets the rate of presynaptic firing, which is the variable that determines whether successive postsynaptic potentials overlap. Receptor number is set by a separate receptor availability control. Resting potential is a property of the postsynaptic cell that this control does not alter. Cleft width is a fixed anatomical feature in the model.

cards.q: In the simulation, what does a receptor blocker control change?
cards.a: The number of postsynaptic receptors available to bind transmitter.
options: The number of transmitter vesicles docked and waiting at the active zone
The speed of action potential conduction along the presynaptic axon
The amount of Ca2+ outside the terminal
The number of postsynaptic receptors available to bind transmitter
cards.explanation: A receptor blocker occupies receptors so fewer are free, which reduces the number of channels that transmitter can open. Docked vesicles belong to the presynaptic release settings. Extracellular Ca2+ is a separate presynaptic variable. Axonal conduction speed is upstream of the synapse and is not what a receptor blocker touches.

cards.q: What units are used on the time axis of the postsynaptic recording in the simulation?
cards.a: Milliseconds.
options: Milliseconds
Seconds
Minutes
Microvolts
cards.explanation: Synaptic events unfold over a few to a few tens of milliseconds, so ms is the scale that makes an EPSP visible. Seconds and minutes are far too coarse and would compress every event into a vertical line. Microvolts are a unit of voltage, not of time.

cards.q: How is the amplitude of an EPSP measured from a simulation trace?
cards.a: As the peak voltage minus the resting baseline voltage, in mV.
options: As the total time the trace is above baseline, in ms
As the peak voltage minus the resting baseline voltage, in mV
As the area under the whole trace
As the difference between threshold and the resting potential
cards.explanation: Amplitude is a height, so it is the number of millivolts from the flat baseline up to the peak of the event. Time above baseline is the duration, a different measurement. Area under the trace is a combined measure of size and duration, not amplitude. The gap between threshold and rest is a fixed property of the cell and does not vary with the EPSP.

cards.q: What does raising the extracellular calcium setting in the simulation affect?
cards.a: The amount of transmitter released per presynaptic action potential.
options: The rate at which transmitter is degraded by enzymes in the cleft
The number of postsynaptic receptors in the membrane
The threshold of the postsynaptic trigger zone
The amount of transmitter released per presynaptic action potential
cards.explanation: Ca2+ entering the terminal triggers vesicle fusion, so more Ca2+ outside means more enters per spike and more transmitter is released. Receptor number is a postsynaptic setting. Threshold is a property of the postsynaptic voltage-gated Na+ channels. Degradation rate is controlled by the enzyme setting, not by Ca2+.

cards.q: On a postsynaptic trace in the simulation, how is an action potential recognized?
cards.a: A rapid spike from threshold to about +30 mV followed by a fast return.
options: A slow drift of the baseline lasting several hundred milliseconds or more
A small 2 mV bump that decays within 15 ms
A rapid spike from threshold to about +30 mV followed by a fast return
A steady hyperpolarization held at -75 mV
cards.explanation: An action potential is an all or none event that overshoots to roughly +30 mV and repolarizes within a couple of milliseconds, so it dwarfs everything else on the trace. A slow baseline drift is usually an artifact or a change in a resting setting. A small decaying bump is a subthreshold EPSP. A maintained hyperpolarization is an inhibitory response.

cards.q: In the simulation the extracellular calcium is set to zero and the presynaptic axon is stimulated. What does the postsynaptic trace show?
cards.a: A flat trace at rest, because no transmitter is released.
options: A normal EPSP, because release does not need Ca2+
An action potential, because the terminal depolarizes
A flat trace at rest, because no transmitter is released
A hyperpolarization below -80 mV
cards.explanation: Vesicle fusion depends on Ca2+ entering the terminal, so with none available nothing is released and the postsynaptic cell sees nothing at all. Release absolutely requires Ca2+, which is the point of the manipulation. The presynaptic terminal does depolarize, but that event is not recorded by the postsynaptic electrode. Nothing in this setting opens inhibitory channels.

cards.q: A student applies enough receptor blocker in the simulation to occupy half the postsynaptic receptors. Compared with the control run, what should the trace show?
cards.a: An EPSP about half as large, with the baseline unchanged.
options: An EPSP twice as large, with the baseline unchanged
An EPSP of normal size, with the baseline shifted down
No EPSP at all and a baseline shifted up
An EPSP about half as large, with the baseline unchanged
cards.explanation: Half the receptors free means about half as many channels open for the same transmitter, so the peak is roughly halved while the resting potential, which does not depend on these receptors, is untouched. A shifted baseline would require channels open at rest. Blocking half the receptors leaves the other half working, so some EPSP remains. Blocking receptors cannot enlarge a response.

cards.q: The simulation is set so that each presynaptic action potential releases twice as many vesicles as the control run. What changes on the postsynaptic trace?
cards.a: The EPSP amplitude increases.
options: The EPSP amplitude increases
The EPSP amplitude decreases
The resting potential becomes more negative
The synaptic delay lengthens noticeably
cards.explanation: More vesicles mean more transmitter, more receptors bound, more channels open, and a larger depolarization, since postsynaptic potentials are graded. Releasing more transmitter cannot shrink the response. Resting potential depends on the leak conductances rather than on how much transmitter arrives. Delay is set by the release machinery and does not lengthen when release increases.

cards.q: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is switched on in the simulation of a cholinergic synapse. What changes in the shape of the postsynaptic potential?
cards.a: It decays more slowly and lasts longer.
options: It decays more quickly and ends sooner
It decays more slowly and lasts longer
It reverses direction and becomes a hyperpolarization
It disappears entirely from the trace
cards.explanation: With the degrading enzyme inhibited, transmitter lingers in the cleft, keeps rebinding, and holds channels open, which stretches out the falling phase. Faster decay would follow from more clearance, not less. The sign of the response depends on which ions the receptor channel passes and is not changed by an enzyme. The response persists and in fact grows, so it does not vanish.

cards.q: In the simulation, the postsynaptic receptor is switched from a Na+ permeable channel to a Cl- permeable channel, with the Cl- equilibrium potential set at -75 mV. What does the trace show after stimulation?
cards.a: A small hyperpolarization, an IPSP.
options: A larger depolarization than before
A small hyperpolarization, an IPSP
An action potential at lower stimulus intensity
No change from the control run
cards.explanation: Cl- entry drives the membrane from -70 mV toward -75 mV, which is a hyperpolarizing, inhibitory response. A larger depolarization would require a channel with a reversal potential above rest. Making the response inhibitory moves the cell away from threshold, so firing becomes harder, not easier. Changing the permeant ion changes the response, so the trace cannot look the same.

cards.q: With single stimuli the simulation produces subthreshold EPSPs. The student raises the stimulus frequency until the EPSPs overlap. What should appear on the trace?
cards.a: The potentials summate, the baseline climbs toward threshold, and an action potential eventually fires.
options: The potentials summate, the baseline climbs toward threshold, and an action potential eventually fires
Each potential stays exactly the same size however close together they arrive, and no action potential ever fires
The potentials cancel one another as they overlap and the trace flattens back to baseline
The resting potential drops toward -90 mV
cards.explanation: When intervals are shorter than the duration of a single EPSP, temporal summation stacks them and the membrane can reach threshold. Potentials stop staying isolated once they overlap, which is the whole point of raising frequency. Two excitatory events add rather than cancel. Nothing in this manipulation opens the K+ conductance that would carry the cell toward -90 mV.

cards.q: In the simulation, EPSP amplitude falls to a third of control. Raising extracellular Ca2+ to twice normal does not restore it, but removing the added drug does. Where is the drug acting?
cards.a: On the postsynaptic receptors.
options: On the presynaptic Ca2+ channels
On the enzyme that clears transmitter
On the postsynaptic receptors
On the presynaptic vesicle fusion proteins
cards.explanation: If more Ca2+ cannot rescue the response, the limiting step is not how much transmitter is released, which leaves the postsynaptic side as the site of action. A block of presynaptic Ca2+ channels would be at least partly overcome by raising extracellular Ca2+. Blocking clearance would enlarge and prolong the response rather than shrink it. A fusion protein defect is presynaptic and would also be helped somewhat by a stronger Ca2+ signal.

cards.q: In a second run, EPSP amplitude again falls to a third of control, but this time raising extracellular Ca2+ restores it to normal. What does this indicate?
cards.a: The manipulation reduced transmitter release, a presynaptic effect.
options: The manipulation removed postsynaptic receptors
The manipulation blocked clearance of transmitter from the cleft
The manipulation raised the postsynaptic threshold
The manipulation reduced transmitter release, a presynaptic effect
cards.explanation: A response that can be rescued by supplying more Ca2+ was limited by how much transmitter was released, which places the effect at the terminal. Missing receptors would not be replaced by extra Ca2+, since the postsynaptic cell would still have too few channels to open. A raised threshold would change firing rather than EPSP amplitude. Blocked clearance would produce a larger, longer response instead of a smaller one.

cards.q: In the simulation a single stimulus gives an 8 mV EPSP, five stimuli at 100 Hz fire an action potential, and five stimuli at 10 Hz do not. Rest is -70 mV and threshold is -55 mV. Explain the difference between the two trains.
cards.a: At 100 Hz the 10 ms interval is shorter than the EPSP duration so the potentials summate, while at 10 Hz each has decayed before the next arrives.
options: At 100 Hz each individual EPSP is larger than at 10 Hz, because a faster train releases more transmitter from every vesicle that fuses, so each one starts higher
At 100 Hz the threshold of the cell falls all the way to the resting potential, so one EPSP is enough
At 10 Hz the EPSPs arrive during the refractory period of the one before and cancel each other out
At 100 Hz the 10 ms interval is shorter than the EPSP duration so the potentials summate, while at 10 Hz each has decayed before the next arrives
cards.explanation: An EPSP lasts roughly 15 ms, so spikes 10 ms apart overlap and add toward the 15 mV needed, while spikes 100 ms apart arrive on a fully recovered baseline. Individual EPSP size depends on transmitter released per spike, not on the interval. An excitatory input does not become inhibitory at lower frequency. Threshold is a fixed property of the trigger zone and does not shift to the resting potential.

cards.q: After a drug is added in the simulation, the postsynaptic baseline shifts from -70 mV to -78 mV and a train that used to fire the cell now produces only summating EPSPs that peak at -60 mV. Interpret both changes.
cards.a: The drug opened an inhibitory conductance, so the cell starts further from threshold and the same excitation no longer reaches it.
options: The drug opened an inhibitory conductance, so the cell starts further from threshold and the same excitation no longer reaches it
The drug raised the threshold of the trigger zone from -55 mV to -60 mV, so the summated EPSPs now fall a few millivolts short of it
The drug blocked presynaptic release, so the events left on the trace are artifacts rather than real EPSPs
The drug removed all of the postsynaptic receptors, so nothing but the shifted baseline is left on the trace
cards.explanation: A hyperpolarized baseline points to new Cl- or K+ channels opening at rest, and starting 8 mV lower means the same summated excitation stops short of the unchanged -55 mV threshold. Nothing in the trace reports a change in threshold itself, and a resting shift explains both observations with one mechanism. Release cannot have been blocked, since EPSPs are still visible. Removing all receptors would leave no EPSPs at all.
